summary:
John Datason is a browser detective game that teaches players how to find, and how to doubt, long-term trends in NASA Earth observation data. The player travels across a toy 3D map of Spain by car, rowing boat and plane. Stopping anywhere and opening the magnifying glass shows six variables for that point: air temperature, a long temperature record, precipitation, soil moisture, evapotranspiration and wind.

Five featured cases (the Valencia DANA floods, Storm Filomena, the Córdoba heat, the Aneto glacier and the Doñana wetlands) start with a witness, guide the player through the evidence chart by chart, and ask for a conclusion before the result is revealed.

Every chart uses the same tested method: monthly anomalies, Sen slope and a pre-whitened Mann-Kendall test at the 5 % level, run on 7,090 series from NASA GLDAS, GPM IMERG and MERRA-2. The game treats "no significant trend" as a real answer and repeats that a trend is not a cause.

This matters because public debate often jumps from one extreme event to a conclusion. We want players to learn to check the long record first.

PROJECT DOCUMENTS

Folder with three PDFs: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1_a3CHjBgpb5t_I0oJuRx-mbpQNT1hc2E?usp=drive_link

- Our tool and its impact on education and on the world (English).

- The same document in Spanish.

- References.

CODE REPOSITORY

https://github.com/nasales/Space-Challange-Na-sales-

WHAT IT DOES

John Datason is a detective game that runs in the browser. The player moves over a 3D map of Spain with real relief, rivers, towns and landmarks. There are two ways to investigate:

1. Any point on the map. Stop, open the magnifying glass and pick one of six clues: air temperature, long-record temperature, precipitation, soil moisture, evapotranspiration or wind. The evidence sheet shows the monthly series, the anomalies with the trend line and its 95 % band, the seasonal cycle, the annual means, and the method and data source.

2. Five featured cases: the Valencia DANA floods, Storm Filomena in Madrid, the Córdoba heat, the Aneto glacier and the Doñana wetlands. A witness gives the context, a case file teaches one way of reading a time series step by step, the player gives a conclusion, and only then the statistical result is revealed.

HOW IT WORKS

Spain is divided into 1,184 land cells of 0.25° (about 28 km). For each cell we store one value per month for six variables, from NASA GLDAS-2.1 Noah (from 2000), GPM IMERG V07 (from 1998) and MERRA-2 (from 1980). That gives 7,090 time series.

Each series gets the same analysis:

- Monthly anomalies: each value minus the mean of its calendar month, so the seasons do not hide or fake a trend.

- Rate of change: Sen slope, per decade, in the units of the variable.

- Significance: Mann-Kendall test with pre-whitening (Yue and Wang, 2002) at the 5 % level, because monthly climate data are autocorrelated and the classic test finds trends that are not there.

- 95 % confidence interval of the slope (Gilbert, 1987).

- At least 120 valid months are required.

WHAT THE DATA SHOW

- Temperature rises almost everywhere: the MERRA-2 record is significant in 1,181 of 1,184 cells, with a median of +0.33 °C per decade.

- Surface soil moisture falls in 54 % of the cells and rises in none.

- Precipitation shows no trend: 2 significant cells out of 1,184, fewer than expected by chance.

- In the Valencia DANA case, precipitation has no significant trend, while temperature rises by 0.31 °C per decade. One extreme event is not a trend, and the game makes the player see that.

HOW WE CHECKED IT

- The whole pipeline was run on 7,104 synthetic series with known answers: the false-positive rate was 4.7-5.6 % (6.8 % for precipitation) and the 95 % interval covered the true slope in 93.9-95.8 % of the series.

- Two team members wrote the trend code separately and the results match to nine decimal places.

- Two independent NASA products (GLDAS and MERRA-2) agree on the sign of the temperature trend in 97 % of the cells.

- We state the limits: short records (26 to 28 years for some variables), 28 km averages, and many tes a region is stronger evidence than one cell.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The game is for students and curious people with no statistics background. It teaches three habits: remove the seasons before looking for change, ask if a change could be chance, and do not confuse a trend with a cause. A

non-significant result is shown as a valid answer, not as a failure.

WHY IT IS CREATIVE

The charts do not give the conclusion. The player has to commit to an answer first, like a detective, and then compare it with the test. The data sit inside a world to explore, with day and night, a boat route to the Canary Islands

and fast travel by plane, instead of a dashboard. [The game can be played in English or Spanish.]

TOOLS

- Game: TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js. Sound effects are synthesised in the browser with the Web Audio API.

- Data and statistics: Python, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, pymannkendall, xarray, earthaccess.

- Database and hosting: Supabase (Postgres), read only from the browser; Cloudflare Workers.

- Tests: pytest and Playwright.
